title: Tenant network activation: bridge-mode reference & terraform shrinkwrap notes
content:
Purpose
This is a working reference for activating tenant networks in bridge-mode (Redwood connectors placed into customer network without full VPC tenancy) and the Terraform module shrinkwrap approach we plan to use to limit drift during upgrades. The doc focuses on activation sequencing, module pinning guidance, compatibility caveats, and an explicit upgrade and rollback play for live customers.

Scope and intended audience
- Audience: field engineers, solutions eng, platform on-call, and infra release owners.
- Scope: activation for private deployments where customers want Redwood to attach via routed/bridge connectors (IP-in-IP/VxLAN or L3 peering) instead of full-provisioned tenant VPC. Includes TF module packaging, acceptance tests, and step-by-step cutover.

Definitions and assumptions
- Bridge-mode: Redwood-managed connectors (VM appliances or k8s DaemonSets) that establish routing/overlay into customer networks. No heavy-handed network resource creation inside customer accounts.
- Shrinkwrap TF modules: a versioned, pinned bundle of Terraform modules + provider versions we deliver to customers for reproducible upgrades.
- Customer prerequisites: a /24 usable subnet for connector placement, BGP session or static routes available, public egress for the connector to reach control plane (or an agreed private peering path), and a cert signing endpoint (ACME or internal CA) if TLS certs are terminated customer-side.

High-level pattern choices (when to use bridge-mode)
- Use bridge-mode when: customer policy forbids our managed VPC resources, customer already has a stable network with transit gateways, or they need minimal IAM scope changes.
- Don't use bridge-mode when: customers require strict tenancy isolation guarantees (air-gapped on-prem with no connectivity to Redwood control plane) or expect us to manage subnet lifecycle.

Connector network design (reference)
- Connector placement: colocate connectors in a dedicated /26 in each AZ (if multi-AZ). For small customer single-AZ, a /28 may suffice.
- Overlay vs L3: prefer VxLAN overlay for predictable MTU (watch overhead) unless customer requires direct L3 peering/BGP for traffic engineering.
- MTU: default to 1400 for overlays. Document the impact to inference payloads (large embeddings or binary chunks) and advise app teams.
- NAT and egress: connectors should have deterministic NAT for outbound calls to our control plane; maintain source IPs for observability and allowlist mapping.
- Firewall rules: allow control-plane port range (see linked Confluence page) and ephemeral ports for telemetry.
- HA: active-active connectors behind an internal LB (health checked). Control-plane affinity via sticky sessions for large KV cache warmups.

Terraform shrinkwrap approach
- Deliverable: a tarball (or private module registry address) containing:
  - Specific module versions (sha pinned)
  - Provider versions >= and <= bounds
  - A small wrapper module that exposes only minimal variables (cidr, asn, bgp_psk, control_plane_endpoints)
- Why shrinkwrap:
  - Prevent inadvertent provider/module upgrades during customer terraform runs.
  - Provide a reproducible path for upgrades where we can test our exact bundle.
- Upgrade cadence and strategy:
  - Minor security fixes: patch in place with a fast-track bump after internal validation.
  - Functional changes (route handling, new NAT behavior): staged rollout per customer with canary connectors.

Compatibility caveats and gotchas
- Provider drift: lock terraform provider versions tightly. Documented issue: aws provider v4.x changed default ENI behaviors affecting MTU and source-dest checks — test explicitly.
- Immutable resources: avoid creating resources that customers commonly modify (route tables, transit gateway attachments) in the shrinkwrap module; instead, document manual steps for customers to attach.
- IP exhaustion: require early IP allocation for connectors so we don't hit address space conflicts during cutover.
- BGP timers: default timers we prefer (3s keepalive / 9s hold) can be aggressive for customer appliances; provide config template with conservative defaults and a recommended tuned set.

Activation checklist (step-by-step)
1) Pre-kickoff (field engineer): collect customer network diagram, ASN, allowed subnets, security contact, and preferred cutover window. Validate CIDR availability.
2) Deliver shrinkwrap bundle and a one-page runbook to the customer. Request a sandbox account/run and ask them to run terraform plan and share the plan output.
3) Test in our staging with identical bundle and run acceptance tests (connectivity matrix below).
4) Provision connectors in staging-customer replica and seed KV cache for common prompt prefixes if applicable.
5) During cutover window:
   a) Apply shrinkwrap in customer account to create connectors (or customer runs it with our guidance).
   b) Validate BGP/session establishment or overlay tunnel health.
   c) Run smoke inference tests: p50/p95 latency, token drop checks, and alignment with expected model variants.
   d) Gradually shift a small % of traffic (5–10%) via routing weight or DNS-based split. Monitor for errors and cost anomalies.
6) Full traffic shift when metrics stable for 30 minutes.
7) Post-cutover: collect telemetry snapshot, export Terraform state, confirm backups, schedule 24h follow-up.

Acceptance tests (automated)
- Connectivity tests: ping/icmp/tcp to control-plane endpoints, BGP session check, traceroutes with expected next-hops.
- Functional tests: small GPT chat request, embedding call, and a streaming response check for correct chunking and reconnect behavior.
- Performance gates: p50 latency <= customer SLO + 10ms, p95 within 2x baseline. Token error rate < 0.1% during ramp.

Upgrade plan (module changes)
- Pre-announce: notify customers 30 days before planned version bump. Include change log and rollback instructions.
- Canary: pick 2 low-risk customers for early rollout. Run full acceptance suite and measure cost/delta.
- Gradual: after canaries pass for 7 days, rollout to additional cohorts in waves (10% -> 25% -> 100%).
- Rollback: keep previous shrinkwrap bundle available; rollback is a re-apply of previous bundle followed by connector restart. Documented caveat: if BGP attributes change, routes may take up to 2x BGP hold timers to converge — plan for that window.

Emergency rollback checklist
- If service errors increase > 2x baseline or p95 latency spikes > 50%:
  - Pause the rollout (stop Terraform apply pipeline).
  - Trigger rollback: apply previous shrinkwrap bundle (operator-run recommended).
  - Verify BGP/overlay sessions reestablished and traffic drained back.

Operational notes for field teams
- Logs: collect connector syslogs and control-plane correlation ids. Keep packet captures for first 30 minutes of cutover if anomalies observed.
- Observability: verify connector-level token-level traces for cost attribution. Confirm that KV cache hits match pre-cutover expectations.
- Support escalation: follow the ERT runbook (linked) and paging matrix; include network on-call and solutions eng.

Open engineering action items
- (Infra) Add a shrinkwrap module generator that emits a bundle + integrity manifest (sha256).
- (SRE) Add synthetic tests that mimic large-sequence inference to validate MTU and fragmentation behavior.
- (DX) Create a one-page customer checklist and a terraform plan linter that flags drift-prone resources.

Appendix: quick config snippets
- BGP minimal template: local-asn: 65000, remote-asn: CUSTOMER_ASN, local-pref: 100, timers: 3/9 (keepalive/hold)
- VxLAN template: vni: 4200, mtu: 1400, encap-overhead: 50 bytes

Notes to self
- Validate the provider version matrix against the latest provider release notes before finalizing the generator.
- Schedule walkthrough with solutions eng and legal for customers with stricter routing policies.

End of draft
